summary: A first-person narrator, apparently a documentary maker, visits a man in white who claims to be a miracle worker in India. She presents her medical test records, which show nothing wrong, and he examines them without much interest. He refuses to say whether he has children, claiming all who come to him are his children, and he reads her as physically unharmonious after placing his hands on her chest. The passage focuses on the setting, his mannerisms, and her growing relaxation and unease.
one_line: A documentary-minded narrator visits a white-robed healer in India, who studies her clean medical records and diagnoses her breathing as disharmonious.
key_facts: The narrator pushes open the door of a room where a man dressed in white sits, apparently meditating.
The man's deep eyes snap open when the narrator enters, and he asks, "Did you bring your records?"
Ramala discreetly disappears while the narrator produces her records from her briefcase.
The room is a sterile baby blue with no diplomas or photos, except a smaller bronze statue of the Dancing Shiva on a silver-inlaid table.
The narrator thinks the man's flowing hair matches that of the bronze figure and concludes that he believes he is Shiva.
The narrator regrets not bringing a Betacam to record video of the man.
The narrator says she has had every test known to science and none found anything wrong.
When asked whether he has children, the man replies, "All those who come here are my children."
The man says, "I haven't examined you yet," and adds that he looks for different things than most physicians.
The man operates a device under his desk that fills the room with a hypnotic drone, which leaves the narrator feeling relaxed and hopeful.
The man places his hands on the narrator's heart, then listens to her chest, and his touch feels warm, then cold, then warm.
The man says, "You're not breathing normally," and "I feel no harmony."
The narrator compares the feeling to her first attempt at Zen meditation in Kyoto.
